options: an increase in enthalpy and entropy
a decrease in enthalpy and entropy
an increase in enthalpy and a decrease in entropy
questions.solution:
The adsorbed molecules lose freedom of movement, so $\Delta S < 0$. For $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ to be negative anyway, $\Delta H$ **must be negative**.

Adsorption is therefore always exothermic, with both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ falling.

questions.q: Which is a feature of chemisorption?
options: It is highly specific and forms a unimolecular layer
It decreases steadily with rising temperature
questions.solution:
Chemisorption involves **chemical bonds**, so it is specific to particular pairs of adsorbent and adsorbate and stops at a **monolayer**.

It is usually irreversible and first rises with temperature, because it needs activation energy. Physisorption is the opposite on each point.

$\dfrac{x}{m} = kP^{1/n}$ with $n > 1$.

In log form, $\log\dfrac{x}{m} = \log k + \dfrac{1}{n}\log P$, a straight line of slope $\dfrac{1}{n}$. It fails at high pressure, where the surface becomes saturated.

questions.q: Activity of iron catalyst is increased by the __________ compound.
questions.solution:
In the Haber process a little $\mathbf{Al_2O_3}$ (with $\mathrm{K_2O}$) acts as a **promoter**, increasing the activity of the iron catalyst.

$\mathrm{H_2S}$ and $\mathrm{As_2O_3}$ do the reverse: they are catalytic poisons.

questions.q: The hydrogenation of vegetable oils using nickel is an example of:
questions.solution:
Solid nickel, liquid oil and gaseous hydrogen are in **different phases**, so this is **heterogeneous catalysis**.

It proceeds by adsorption: $\mathrm{H_2}$ is adsorbed and dissociated on the nickel surface, then adds across the C=C bonds of the oil.

questions.q: The Tyndall effect is shown by:
questions.solution:
Colloidal particles (1–1000 nm) are large enough to **scatter light**, making the beam's path visible.

The particles of a true solution are too small to scatter visibly, which is how the effect tells a sol from a solution.

questions.q: In an electrical field, the particles of a Colloidal system move towards cathode. The coagulation of the same sol is studied using (i) $\mathrm{K_2SO_4}$, (ii) $\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}$, (iii) $\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$ and (iv) NaCl. Their coagulating power should be :
questions.solution:
Particles that move to the cathode are **positively** charged, so the anions do the coagulating.

Hardy–Schulze rule: the higher the charge on the anion, the greater the power. $[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6}]^{4-} > \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}} > \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} > \mathrm{Cl^-}$, which is **(iii) > (ii) > (i) > (iv)**.

**Butter is a gel**: liquid dispersed in a solid.

The others are mismatched: mist is an aerosol of a liquid, smoke is an aerosol of a solid, and whipped cream is a foam (gas in liquid).

questions.q: Brownian movement in colloidal particles is caused by:
options: unequal bombardment by molecules of the dispersion medium
questions.solution:
Molecules of the medium strike each particle **unequally** from different sides at every instant, so the particle is pushed in a random zigzag.

This constant motion stirs the sol and helps stop the particles settling.

questions.q: In a plot of $\log\dfrac{x}{m}$ against $\log P$ for Freundlich adsorption, the slope is $0.5$. Find $n$.
For an adsorption obeying $\dfrac{x}{m} = kP^{1/2}$, by what factor does $\dfrac{x}{m}$ increase when the pressure is increased four times?
The diameter of colloidal particles lies between $1\,\mathrm{nm}$ and how many nanometres?
questions.solution:
Colloidal particles range from about $\mathbf{1}$ **to** $\mathbf{1000\,nm}$.

Below 1 nm the mixture is a true solution; above 1000 nm it is a suspension whose particles settle.

questions.q: An adsorption obeys $\dfrac{x}{m} = kP^{1/3}$. By what factor does $\dfrac{x}{m}$ increase when the pressure is increased eight times?
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{(x/m)_2}{(x/m)_1} = 8^{1/3} = \mathbf{2}$.

An eightfold rise in pressure only doubles the amount adsorbed: with $n > 1$ the surface fills ever more slowly as it approaches saturation.

questions.q: $2\,\mathrm{g}$ of charcoal adsorbs $0.6\,\mathrm{g}$ of acetic acid from solution. Find $\dfrac{x}{m}$.
questions.solution: $\dfrac{x}{m} = \dfrac{0.6}{2} = \mathbf{0.3}$, the mass adsorbed per gram of adsorbent.

questions.q: Explain how colloidal sols are purified by dialysis and electrodialysis, and describe two methods of preparing colloids: Bredig's arc method and peptisation.
questions.solution:
**Why purify.** A freshly made sol carries dissolved electrolytes. A small amount stabilises it, but an excess coagulates it.

**Dialysis.** The sol is placed in a bag of parchment or cellophane, a membrane that lets ions and small molecules through but holds back colloidal particles. The bag hangs in running water, and the electrolytes diffuse out.

**Electrodialysis.** Dialysis is slow, so electrodes are placed either side of the membrane. The applied field pulls the ions out much faster. It works only when the impurity is an electrolyte.

**Bredig's arc method** (dispersion). An electric arc is struck between two metal electrodes held under water containing a little KOH. The heat vaporises the metal, which condenses into colloidal particles. It is used for gold, silver and platinum sols.

**Peptisation** (dispersion). A freshly made precipitate is turned into a sol by shaking it with a small amount of an electrolyte, the peptising agent. The precipitate adsorbs one of its ions, the particles become like-charged and push each other apart. For example, fresh $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$ with a little $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ adsorbs $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ and gives a positive sol.
